questions_and_answers.question_text: What are the two meanings of bú cuò?
What are the three parts of a three-part verb?
How does zěnme differ from wèishénme?
What does rènshi mean as a state verb, and as an action verb?
How do rènshi and zhīdao differ when a person is discussed?
What does rènshi mean when a PLACE is discussed?

answers.answer_text: "To know how to get there" — while zhīdao continues to mean "to know of" a place.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Contrast Nǐ zěnme lái le? with Nǐ shi zěnme láide?

answers.answer_text: The first means "How come you are here?"; the second means "How did you get here?" (by what means of transportation).

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I met him the year before last."
Write the Chinese for "I know of her, but we haven't met."

answers.answer_text: Wǒ zhīdao ta, dànshi wǒmen méi jiànguo.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "How many Chinese characters do you recognize?"

articles.text:
4. B: Bú cuò, Fāng Démíng shi        That's right. Fāng Démíng was sent
      shàngge lǐbài pài dào           over here last week.
      wǒmen zhèli láide.
   B: Zěnme? Nǐ rènshi ta ma?        Why? Do you know him?

Notes on No. 4

Bú cuò means "not bad" in the sense of "pretty good," "pretty well," "all right." In the first sentence of No. 4, bú cuò means "that's right, your information is not wrong."

Nǐ zěnmeyàng?                    How are things going?
Bú cuò.                          Not bad.
Nèige fànguǎnzide cài zhēn       That restaurant really has pretty
bú cuò.                          good food.

Pài dào...lái is a THREE-PART VERB: action verb (also expressing motion), prepositional verb (must take an object), and directional verb (lái, qù).

ACTION VERB | PREPOSITIONAL VERB | OBJECT | DIRECTIONAL VERB
pǎo         | dào                | shānshang | qù   ("run up the hill")
bān         | dào                | zhèr      | lái  ("move into here")
pài         | dào                | wǒmen zhèli | lái ("send over here")
zǒu         | dào                | hòubianr  | lái  ("walk to the back")

Zěnme, "why," "how come," "how is it that...," is a more colloquial and challenging word for "why" than wèishénme. Only a reason or an explanation is requested by wèishénme. Zěnme expresses more, emphasizing the speaker's surprise or lack of understanding.

Nǐmende bàngōngshì zěnme         How is it that your office is so
zhème xiǎo?                      small?
Nǐ zěnme bú niàn shū ne?         How come you're not studying?

The meaning of zěnme is sometimes affected by the aspect marker used:

Nǐ zěnme lái le?                 How come you are here? (i.e., "What
                                 are you doing here?")
Nǐ (shi) zěnme láide?            How did you get here? (i.e., by what
                                 means of transportation)

Rènshi as a STATE VERB means "to know" in the sense of "to be acquainted with," "to be familiar with," "to recognize." As an ACTION VERB, rènshi means "to meet," "to get acquainted with."

(STATE VERB)
Nǐ rènshi tā ma?                 Do you know him?
Wǒmen bú tài rènshi.             We are not too well acquainted.

(ACTION VERB)
Wǒ shi qiánnián rènshi tāde.     I met him the year before last.
Nèige shíhou wǒmen hái méi       At that time we had not yet met.
rènshi.

As a state verb, rènshi is used for "knowing" or "recognizing" Chinese characters.

Nǐ rènshi duōshaoge Zhōngguo     How many Chinese characters do you
zì?                              know/recognize?

Contrast the meanings of rènshi and zhīdao: rènshi, "to know" a person; zhīdao, "to know OF" a person.

Nǐ rènshi Táng Xiǎojiě ma?       Do you know Miss Táng?
Wǒ zhīdao ta, dànshi wǒmen       I know of her, but we haven't met.
méi jiànguo.

When a PLACE is being discussed, rènshi means "to know how to get (there)." Zhīdao continues to mean "to know of (a place)."

Nǐ rènshi nèige diànyǐngyuàn     Do you know how to get to that movie
ma?                              theater?
Nǐ zhīdao nèige diànyǐngyuàn     Do you know of that movie theater?
ma?
